title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: The officers were about to leave, but Prince Andrew, apparently reluctant to be left alone with his friend, asked them to stay and have tea. Seats were brought and tea was served. The officers gazed with surprise at Pierre's huge, stout figure and listened to his talk about Moscow and the position of their army, around which he had ridden. Prince Andrew remained silent, and his expression was so forbidding that Pierre directed his remarks mainly to the good-natured battalion commander.
"So you understand the whole layout of our troops?" Prince Andrew interrupted him.
"Yes—that is, how do you mean?" said Pierre. "Not being a military man, I can't say I've fully understood it, but I get the general picture."
"Well then, you know more than anyone else, whoever that may be," said Prince Andrew.
"Oh!" said Pierre, looking over his spectacles in perplexity at Prince Andrew. "Well, and what do you think about Kutuzov's appointment?" he asked.
"I was very glad of his appointment, that's all I know," replied Prince Andrew.
"And tell me your opinion of Barclay de Tolly. In Moscow they're saying all sorts of things about him... What do you think of him?"
"Ask them," replied Prince Andrew, indicating the officers.
Pierre looked at Timokhin with the condescendingly inquiring smile that everyone involuntarily used when addressing that officer.
"We can see the light again since his Serenity's been appointed, your excellency," said Timokhin timidly, continually glancing at his colonel.
"Why so?" asked Pierre.

"Well, take just firewood and fodder, for example. Why, when we were retreating from Sventsyani, we didn't dare touch a stick or a wisp of hay or anything. You see, we were leaving, so he'd get it all; isn't that right, your excellency?" and Timokhin again looked at the prince. "But we didn't dare. In our regiment two officers were court-martialed for that kind of thing. But once his Serenity took command, everything became straightforward. Now we can see the light..."
"Then why was it forbidden?"
Timokhin looked about in confusion, not knowing how to answer. Pierre put the same question to Prince Andrew.

"So as not to lay waste the country we were leaving to the enemy," said Prince Andrew with bitter irony. "It's very sound: you can't allow the land to be pillaged or accustom the troops to looting. At Smolensk too he calculated correctly that the French might outflank us since they had larger forces. But he couldn't understand this," cried Prince Andrew in a shrill voice that seemed to escape him involuntarily: "he couldn't understand that there, for the first time, we were fighting for Russian soil, and that there was a spirit in the men such as I had never seen before, and that we had held the French for two days, and that that success had increased our strength tenfold. He ordered us to retreat, and all our efforts and losses went for nothing. He didn't intend to betray us; he tried to do his best; he thought out everything carefully—and that is exactly why he's unfit. He's unfit now precisely because he plans everything very thoroughly and precisely, as every German must. How can I explain it?... Well, say your father has a German valet, and the valet is excellent and satisfies your father's needs better than you could—then it's fine to let him serve. But if your father is mortally ill, you'll send the valet away and attend to your father with your own clumsy, unpracticed hands, and will comfort him better than a skilled stranger could. That's how it's been with Barclay. While Russia was healthy, a foreigner could serve her and be a splendid minister; but the moment she's in danger, she needs one of her own. But in your Club they've been calling him a traitor! They've slandered him as a traitor, and the only result will be that later, ashamed of their false accusations, they'll suddenly make him out to be a hero or genius instead—and that will be even more unjust. He is an honest and very meticulous German."
"And they say he's a skillful commander," Pierre remarked.
"I don't understand what 'a skillful commander' means," replied Prince Andrew ironically.
"A skillful commander?" said Pierre. "Well, one who foresees all possibilities... and anticipates the enemy's intentions."
"But that's impossible," said Prince Andrew, as if it were a long-settled matter.
Pierre looked at him in surprise.
"And yet they say war is like a game of chess?" he remarked.

"Yes," replied Prince Andrew, "but with this little difference: in chess you can think over each move as long as you like and aren't limited by time, and with this further difference, that a knight is always stronger than a pawn and two pawns are always stronger than one—while in war a battalion is sometimes stronger than a division and sometimes weaker than a company. The relative strength of bodies of troops can never be known to anyone. Believe me," he continued, "if things depended on plans made by the staff, I would be there making plans. But instead I have the honor of serving here in the regiment with these gentlemen, and I believe that on us—not on those others—tomorrow's battle will depend... Success never has depended, and never will depend, on position, equipment, or even numbers—and least of all on position."
"But on what then?"
"On the feeling that is in me and in him," he pointed to Timokhin, "and in every soldier."

Prince Andrew glanced at Timokhin, who looked at his commander in alarm and confusion. In contrast to his former reserved taciturnity, Prince Andrew now seemed stirred up. He apparently couldn't stop himself from expressing the thoughts that had suddenly taken hold of him.

"A battle is won by those who firmly resolve to win it! Why did we lose the battle of Austerlitz? Our losses were nearly equal to the French, but very early we told ourselves we were losing the battle—and we lost it. And we said so because we had nothing to fight for there, we wanted to get away from the battlefield as fast as possible. 'We've lost, so let's run,' and we ran. If we hadn't said that till evening, God knows what might have happened. But tomorrow we won't say it! You talk about our position—the left flank weak, the right flank overextended," he went on. "That's all nonsense, none of it matters. But what awaits us tomorrow? A hundred million totally unpredictable circumstances that will be decided in an instant by whether our men or theirs run or don't run, and whether this man or that man is killed. Everything being done now is just play. The fact is that those men you've been riding around with don't just fail to help—they actually hinder. They're only concerned with their own petty interests."
"At such a moment?" said Pierre reproachfully.

"At such a moment!" Prince Andrew repeated. "To them it's only an opportunity to undermine a rival and earn an extra medal or ribbon. For me, tomorrow means this: a Russian army of a hundred thousand and a French army of a hundred thousand have met to fight, and the point is that these two hundred thousand men will fight, and whichever side fights more fiercely and spares itself less will win. And if you want to know: whatever happens, whatever blunders those at the top may make, we will win tomorrow's battle. Tomorrow, happen what may, we will win!"

"That's right, your excellency! That's the truth, the real truth," said Timokhin. "Who would spare himself now? The soldiers in my battalion—believe me—won't touch their vodka! 'It's not the day for that!' they say."

Everyone fell silent. The officers rose. Prince Andrew went out of the shed with them, giving final orders to the adjutant. After they had gone, Pierre approached Prince Andrew and was about to start talking when they heard the clatter of three horses on the road nearby. Looking in that direction, Prince Andrew recognized Wolzogen and Clausewitz accompanied by a Cossack. They rode close by, still talking, and Prince Andrew involuntarily caught these words:
"The war must be extended across a wide area. I cannot praise that view highly enough," said one of them.
* "The war must be extended widely. I cannot sufficiently commend that view."
"Oh yes," said the other, "the only objective is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot take into account the loss of private individuals."
* "Oh yes, the only aim is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot consider the loss of private individuals."
"Oh, no," agreed the other.

"Extend widely!" said Prince Andrew with an angry snort when they had ridden past. "In that 'extend' were my father, son, and sister at Bald Hills. That's all the same to him! That's what I was telling you—those German gentlemen won't win the battle tomorrow, they'll only make as big a mess as they can, because they have nothing in their German heads but theories not worth an empty eggshell, and haven't in their hearts the one thing needed tomorrow—the thing Timokhin has. They've surrendered all of Europe to him, and now they've come to teach us. Fine teachers!" and again his voice went shrill.
"So you think we'll win tomorrow's battle?" asked Pierre.

"Yes, yes," answered Prince Andrew absently. "One thing I would do if I had the power," he began again, "I would not take prisoners. Why take prisoners? It's playing at chivalry! The French have destroyed my home and are on their way to destroy Moscow; they have outraged and continue to outrage me every moment. They are my enemies. In my view they are all criminals. And Timokhin thinks so too, and the whole army. They should be executed! Since they are my enemies, they cannot be my friends, whatever may have been said at Tilsit."
"Yes, yes," muttered Pierre, looking with shining eyes at Prince Andrew. "I completely agree with you!"

The question that had troubled Pierre on the Mozhaysk hill and throughout the day now seemed perfectly clear and fully resolved. He now understood the whole meaning and importance of this war and of the coming battle. Everything he had seen that day, all the significant and serious expressions on the faces he had passed, were illuminated for him by a new light. He understood that latent heat (as they say in physics) of patriotism which was present in all these men he had seen, and this explained why they all prepared for death calmly and almost lightheartedly.

"Not take prisoners," Prince Andrew continued. "That alone would completely change the whole war and make it less cruel. As it is, we've been playing at war—that's what's vile! We play at magnanimity and all that stuff. Such magnanimity and sensitivity are like a lady who faints at the sight of a calf being slaughtered: she is so tenderhearted she can't look at blood, but she enjoys eating the calf served up with sauce. They talk to us about the rules of war, about chivalry, about flags of truce, about mercy to the unfortunate, and so on. It's all rubbish! I saw chivalry and flags of truce in 1805; they deceived us and we deceived them. They plunder other people's homes, circulate counterfeit money, and worst of all they kill my children and my father—and then talk about rules of war and magnanimity to the enemy! Take no prisoners, kill and be killed! Whoever has come to this, as I have, through the same suffering..."

Prince Andrew, who had thought it made no difference to him whether Moscow was taken as Smolensk had been, was suddenly checked by an unexpected cramp in his throat. He paced back and forth a few times in silence, but his eyes glittered feverishly and his lips quivered as he began speaking.

"If there were none of this magnanimity in war, we would go to war only when it was worth going to certain death, as now. Then there would be no war because Paul Ivanovich had offended Michael Ivanovich. And when there was a war like this one, it would be real war! And then the determination of the troops would be completely different. Then all these Westphalians and Hessians whom Napoleon is dragging along would not follow him into Russia, and we would not go fight in Austria and Prussia without knowing why. War is not a polite game but the most horrible thing in life; and we ought to understand that and not play at it. We ought to accept this terrible necessity sternly and seriously. It all comes down to this: get rid of the falsehood and let war be war and not a game. As it is now, war is the favorite pastime of the idle and frivolous. The military profession is the most highly honored."

"But what is war? What is needed for success in warfare? What are the customs of the military? The aim of war is murder; the methods of war are spying, treachery, and their encouragement, the ruin of a country's inhabitants, robbing them or stealing to feed the army, and fraud and falsehood called military strategy. Military life means the absence of freedom—that is, discipline—plus idleness, ignorance, cruelty, debauchery, and drunkenness. And in spite of all this, it is the most esteemed class, respected by everyone. All the kings except the Chinese wear military uniforms, and the man who kills the most people gets the highest rewards."

"They gather, as we shall gather tomorrow, to murder one another; they kill and maim tens of thousands, and then hold thanksgiving services for having killed so many people (they even exaggerate the numbers), and announce a victory, supposing that the more people killed, the greater the achievement. How does God above look down at them and hear them?" exclaimed Prince Andrew in a shrill, piercing voice. "Ah, my friend, it has become hard for me to live of late. I see that I have begun to understand too much. And it isn't good for man to taste of the tree of knowledge of good and evil... Well, it won't be for much longer!" he added.
"However, you're sleepy, and it's time for me to sleep. Go back to Gorki!" said Prince Andrew suddenly.
"Oh no!" Pierre replied, looking at Prince Andrew with frightened, compassionate eyes.
"Go, go! Before a battle one needs a good night's sleep," repeated Prince Andrew.
He came quickly up to Pierre, embraced and kissed him. "Goodbye, be off!" he shouted. "Whether we meet again or not..." and turning away abruptly, he went into the shed.
It was already dark, and Pierre could not tell whether the expression on Prince Andrew's face was angry or tender.

For some time he stood in silence, wondering whether he should follow him or go away. "No, he doesn't want me to!" Pierre decided. "And I know that this is our last meeting!" He sighed deeply and rode back to Gorki.
Re-entering the shed, Prince Andrew lay down on a rug, but he could not sleep.

He closed his eyes. One image succeeded another in his imagination. On one of them he dwelt long and joyfully. He vividly recalled an evening in Petersburg. Natasha, with an animated, excited face, was telling him how she had gone looking for mushrooms the previous summer and had gotten lost in the big forest. She described the depths of the forest, her feelings, and a conversation with a beekeeper she met, incoherently and constantly interrupting her story to say: "No, I can't! I'm not telling it right; no, you don't understand," though he encouraged her by saying that he did understand, and he really had understood all she wanted to say. But Natasha was not satisfied with her own words: she felt they didn't convey the passionately poetic feeling she had experienced that day and wished to share. "He was such a delightful old man, and it was so dark in the forest... and he had such kind... No, I can't describe it," she had said, flushed and excited. Prince Andrew smiled now the same happy smile as he had then when he looked into her eyes. "I understood her," he thought. "I not only understood her, but it was that inner, spiritual force—that sincerity, that openness of soul—that very soul of hers, which seemed bound by her body—it was that soul I loved in her... loved so deeply and happily..." and suddenly he remembered how his love had ended. "He didn't need anything like that. He neither saw nor understood anything of the kind. He only saw in her a pretty, fresh young girl with whom he didn't bother to join his fate. And I?... and he is still alive and happy!"
Prince Andrew jumped up as if someone had burned him, and again began pacing back and forth in front of the shed.
